title: Nothing fixed (section 7)
hook: has the Tathagata attained anything? there is no fixed thing called the highest awakening

segments.voice: Yesterday, the raft again: the teaching is for crossing, not for carrying on your head. Your line: even the raft. Which rule did you set down on the bank? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

A test question, with a trap folded inside it. The Buddha asks Subhuti two things. Has the Tathagata attained the highest, complete awakening? And has the Tathagata taught any teaching? Any student in that room could answer on reflex. Yes, and yes. That's the whole story, isn't it? A seeker sits down under a tree, wakes up, and spends the rest of his life teaching what he found. Subhuti has been listening to this sutra, though, and he doesn't answer on reflex. He answers more carefully than that. Today: nothing fixed.
screen: `TWO QUESTIONS.` → `THE REFLEX ANSWER: YES AND YES.` → `SUBHUTI ANSWERS MORE CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: First, the question itself. The Buddha asks whether he has attained the highest awakening, and whether he has taught a teaching. In the sutra's Sanskrit, that awakening has a long, grand name: anuttara samyak sambodhi, awakening that's complete, with nothing above it. Second, Subhuti's answer. As I understand what the Buddha has taught, he says, there is no fixed thing called the highest awakening. And there is no fixed teaching that the Tathagata has taught. No fixed thing. That's the phrase to hold on to, lightly. Third, the reason he gives. What the Tathagata has taught, Subhuti says, can't be grasped and can't be spoken. It isn't a thing, and it isn't a no-thing either. Then a short line closes the section: the wise and holy ones are all set apart by the unconditioned, by what isn't put together from parts. Fourth, what this is not saying. It isn't saying the Buddha never woke up, or that he taught nothing, or that the teaching is empty talk. The rest of the sutra is a teaching, after all, and Subhuti is learning from it. What it's saying is that awakening isn't an object he picked up and put in his pocket, something with edges you could hand over. Waking up in the morning isn't something you keep in a drawer, either. The same goes for smaller certainties. I'm the responsible one. She never listens. This job is who I am. Each one is useful. Each one, held as a fixed thing, starts to harden. The sutra keeps the hand open, even around the highest thing it knows.
screen: `HAS HE ATTAINED ANYTHING?` · `NO FIXED THING CALLED AWAKENING.` · `NOT GRASPED, NOT SPOKEN.` · `NOT AN OBJECT IN A POCKET.` · then, large: `NOTHING FIXED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: hold one certainty loosely. Settle, and let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up. Breathe. Bring to mind one thing you're sure of, about yourself or about someone close to you. Say it once, quietly, inside. Now notice how you're holding it. Like a fist, or like water in cupped hands? You don't have to drop it or argue with it. Just let the grip ease by one degree, the way your palms are already open. When it tightens again, notice, and open again. The bell holds the time.
Nothing fixed. There is no fixed thing called the highest awakening, and no fixed teaching; what the Buddha taught can't be grasped. Today's word.
Your line: nothing fixed. Today, when you hear yourself say always or never about someone, add the word lately, and see if it's truer. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Teachers in Mahayana schools, Zen among them, use this section to point out that awakening is not a possession to be gained.

fork.setup: you're Subhuti. the Buddha asks: has the Tathagata attained the highest awakening, and has he taught any teaching? what do you answer?
options: yes and yes: that's the whole story.
there's no fixed thing called awakening, and no fixed teaching.
no: the Buddha attained nothing and taught nothing.
fork.reveal: Subhuti says there is no fixed thing called the highest awakening and no fixed teaching: what was taught can't be grasped or spoken, and is neither a thing nor a no-thing.

original.note: Sanskrit: unsurpassed, complete awakening; the sutra's name for what the Buddha awoke to.

trapdoor: what you thought: awakening is a prize the Buddha won and kept.
what it means: there's no fixed thing called the highest awakening; what was taught can't be grasped or spoken.
what a scholar hears: anuttara samyak sambodhi, held with an open hand: neither a thing nor a no-thing, a teaching that refuses to become an object.
recall: a factor that colors the knowing

notes: Section numbering follows the common 32-section division of Kumarajiva's Chinese text.

The closing line of section 7 (all sages differ by / are distinguished by the unconditioned) is rendered 'set apart by the unconditioned'; translators read it differently, so a Keeper should check the gloss.
Original: Devanagari spelling of anuttara samyaksambodhi (nominative form shown) should be checked.
Editor pass: rewrote the unclear clock comparison ('closer to how being awake is different from owning a clock') and dropped the stock 'on an ordinary Tuesday' turn repeated across this range.
